changes.before: In this work, hybrid key establishment combines classical and post-quantum cryptographic mechanisms to reduce reliance on either component alone during the transition to quantum-resistant security. This combination increases the communication cost of tree-based group messaging, while changing the tree arity introduces a separate cost of rebuilding shared state. This paper investigates a migration policy for hybrid TreeKEM that increases arity from two to four and, conceptually, from four to eight. Each valid node carries classical and post-quantum key material. During migration, the new tree becomes the sole source of the group commit secret, while an authenticated cover of eligible old-tree nodes temporarily delivers new path secrets. Subsequent commits populate the new tree, and normalized delivery costs guide retirement of the old cover. An analytical model accounts for public-key and encapsulation payload separately from other protocol fields. Under its healthy-tree approximation, increasing arity from two to four at 129 members reduces the modeled payload from 12,672 to 6,976 bytes, a 44.9% reduction. A leaf-only initial transition at 1,024 members instead requires eleven additional healthy commits to recover its modeled excess cost. Security is examined through conditional arguments rather than a formal proof. Retained old keys can prolong group-wide exposure after compromise, so a communication-cost threshold does not establish cryptographic recovery. The contribution is a migration design and explicit accounting of its efficiency and security tradeoffs.
changes.after: Hybrid key establishment combines classical and post-quantum cryptography to reduce reliance on either component alone during the transition to quantum-resistant communication. TreeKEM is the tree-based group key establishment mechanism used by Messaging Layer Security (MLS) to refresh shared keys as group membership changes. Combining both types of cryptography increases the size of key updates. We propose a migration mechanism that changes the number of children per internal node from two to four and considers a later change to eight. During a transition, members use suitable keys from the old tree to encrypt the secret values needed to establish keys in the new tree. Subsequent updates establish additional internal keys, and a communication-cost criterion determines when to discard the old tree. For a balanced tree with all required internal keys available, our analysis estimates that changing from two to four children at 129 members reduces the public-key and encapsulation data per update from 12,672 to 6,976 bytes, or 44.9%. These figures exclude other message fields. In a separate example with 1,024 members, a transition that encrypts separately for every other member requires eleven later updates at the assumed steady cost to recover its additional cost. The security evaluation explains why retaining old keys can delay recovery after compromise and states the assumptions behind the security argument.

changes.before: Chevalier et al. study tree evolution and degree selection for MLS [3]. A broader comparison should use the same topology assumptions and cost model across several candidate degrees.

changes.before: Retirement must be an authenticated state change accepted consistently by remaining members, followed by removal of the retained old-key envelope. Cost authorization alone cannot perform this change. Nor does local erasure delete copies obtained by an adversary. The informal update windows in the thesis are planning heuristics and do not establish a fixed number of commits for either retirement or security recovery.

changes.before: Forward secrecy requires protection of earlier traffic after later state compromise. One-way path derivation and erasure of obsolete state support this goal only under an appropriate key-evolution argument. TreeCover deliberately extends the lifetime of some old private keys. A later compromise of a retained key may expose recorded migration ciphertexts addressed to that key. Whether those recovered path secrets expose a particular earlier epoch additionally depends on the key-schedule state available to the adversary. Retention therefore changes the relevant exposure window and cannot be dismissed as a harmless storage optimization.
changes.after: Forward secrecy requires protection of earlier traffic after later state compromise. One-way path derivation and erasure of obsolete state support this goal only under an appropriate key-evolution argument. Retaining the old tree deliberately extends the lifetime of some old private keys. A later compromise of a retained key may expose recorded migration ciphertexts addressed to that key. Whether those recovered path secrets expose a particular earlier epoch additionally depends on the key-schedule state available to the adversary. Retention therefore changes the relevant exposure window and cannot be dismissed as a harmless storage optimization.

changes.before: Consider an attacker that copied a member's state, including an old cover private key and the relevant preceding epoch state. If a later commit still encrypts a useful new-tree path secret to that old key, the attacker can recover it and derive upward to the new root. With the necessary previous key-schedule inputs, the attacker can continue deriving group epoch state. The disclosure is not confined to the leaves below that old node: the recovered root contribution affects the group's common secret.

changes.before: The design shifts part of an arity change from an immediate rebuild into subsequent ordinary commits. TreeCover provides a concrete way to make that shift: old internal keys can reduce leaf-level delivery while the new tree acquires usable internal state. The same retained keys prolong dependencies on historical secrets. Communication efficiency and compromise recovery must therefore be treated as separate objectives, even when both motivate refreshing tree state.
changes.after: The design shifts part of an arity change from an immediate rebuild into subsequent ordinary commits. Retaining the old tree provides a way to make that shift: old internal keys can reduce leaf-level delivery while the new tree acquires usable internal state. The same retained keys prolong dependencies on historical secrets. Communication efficiency and compromise recovery must therefore be treated as separate objectives, even when both motivate refreshing tree state.

changes.before: The analytical savings show where the chosen parameter dimensions can make a higher arity attractive. They do not determine the best arity or threshold. A broader analytical treatment should include ternary and other degrees, exact occupied topology, heterogeneous update frequencies, repeated removals, and cumulative costs over both growing and shrinking groups. Fixed-degree, immediate-rebuild, and TreeCover policies should be compared for the same mathematical sequence of group changes, with setup, Welcome, and retirement costs included.
changes.after: The analytical savings show where the chosen parameter dimensions can make a higher arity attractive. They do not determine the best arity or threshold. A broader analytical treatment should include ternary and other degrees, exact occupied topology, heterogeneous update frequencies, repeated removals, and cumulative costs over both growing and shrinking groups. Fixed-degree policies, immediate rebuilding, and policies that temporarily retain the old tree should be compared for the same mathematical sequence of group changes, with setup, Welcome, and retirement costs included.

changes.before: The most urgent protocol work is to finalize the thesis combiner, its encodings, and the state-transition rules. A security model must track historical node-key knowledge during migration, distinguish passive post-quantum confidentiality from active authentication, and define the conditions for recovery. A formal treatment should include authenticated tree-version agreement, removal eligibility, and atomic retirement at each receiver. The present conditional analysis identifies these obligations without claiming that they have been discharged.
changes.after: The most urgent protocol work is to finalize the hybrid combiner, its encodings, and the state-transition rules. A formal treatment should include authenticated tree-version agreement, removal eligibility, and atomic retirement at each receiver. changes.before: The analytical scope also has limits. The healthy reference replaces exact occupied topology by a rounded-height approximation, while the break-even examples assume immediate healthy operation after transition. A tighter analysis would bound the cumulative delivery cost while the new tree remains sparse and would specify how changes in membership affect those bounds. Such a result is not supplied by the present examples.
changes.after: The analytical scope also has limits. The fully populated reference replaces exact occupied topology by a rounded-height approximation, while the break-even examples assume that the new tree immediately operates at the fully populated reference cost. A tighter analysis would bound the cumulative delivery cost while the new tree remains sparse and would specify how changes in membership affect those bounds. Such a result is not supplied by the present examples.

changes.before: Adaptive arity in hybrid TreeKEM is useful only if the costs and security consequences of changing the tree are included. The thesis design makes the new root authoritative immediately and uses an old-tree TreeCover to deliver new path secrets during gradual population. Its reference model exhibits lower mature-tree key-and-KEM payload at selected larger arities, while the transition examples show that repaying initial cost can require many later commits. These analytical examples do not prove the construction secure or establish that one migration policy has lower cumulative cost for every sequence of group changes. TreeCover is therefore best understood as a migration mechanism whose efficiency policy must be complemented by explicit key-freshness, authentication, and recovery conditions.
changes.after: Adaptive arity in hybrid TreeKEM is useful only if the costs and security consequences of changing the tree are included. The proposed mechanism uses the new root to determine the group's fresh secret contribution and temporarily retains keys from the old tree to encrypt new path secrets while internal keys are established. Its reference model exhibits lower mature-tree key-and-KEM payload at selected larger arities, while the transition examples show that repaying initial cost can require many later commits. These analytical examples do not prove the construction secure or establish that one migration policy has lower cumulative cost for every sequence of group changes. Its communication savings must therefore be evaluated together with key freshness, authentication, and the conditions for recovery.
